# Piecewise-softmax exact contact martingale allocations

This is a finite-dimensional regularization theorem for an ALREADY
feasible contact martingale. It does not prove new transport feasibility,
depth, body stationarity, or a Gamma bound. Its boundary traces can be
used in later arguments only with their actual interface jumps retained.

## 1. Data and conclusion

Let S be finitely many positive compact convex d-dimensional fibers
{z} times K_z in a finite-dimensional affine space, and C=conv S. Let

    L(w)=min_(r=1,...,R) A_r(w)>0 on C

be finite-PL concave, M the original mixed volume, and
dnu=dm/(M L). No logarithmic normalization is needed. Choose finitely
many marked sources Y_i in C and positive masses m_i. Assume a feasible
measurable allocation q_i^0 exists with

    q_i^0>=0,  sum_i q_i^0=1 nu-a.e.,
    integral q_i^0 dnu=m_i,
    integral w q_i^0 dnu=m_i Y_i,                       (1)

and q_i^0 supported where EVERY plane active at Y_i touches L. Zero-mass
source labels, if initially listed, may be deleted.

Then there is an allocation satisfying exactly the same (1) and contacts
which has the following form. Subdivide each fiber by finitely many affine
hyperplanes. On every positive-volume chamber the allowed label set I is
constant, and ONE finite global collection of affine scores s_i(w) gives

    q_i(w)=1_(i in I) exp(s_i(w))/sum_(j in I)exp(s_j(w)).       (2)

Thus q_i has an ambient real-analytic extension from each chamber to its
closure, with bounded derivatives of every fixed order. After refining
also by the PL cells of L, the row density q_i/(M L) has the same property.
Bounds depend on the given moment data and need not be uniform along a
family approaching a new face of the feasible moment range.

For curved convex K_z, a chamber means K_z intersected with an affine
polyhedral region. It is a literal polytope only when K_z is polytopal.
No assertion replaces a curved boundary by finitely many flat facets.

## 2. Initial contacts and the compact moment range

For each source let R_i={r:A_r(Y_i)=L(Y_i)}. Its contact set is

    E_i=C intersect intersection_(r in R_i, s=1,...,R)
                                      {A_r<=A_s}.       (3)

This is the intersection of C with finitely many affine halfspaces.
Indeed the inequalities say exactly that every A_r in R_i attains the
minimum L. Put I_0(w)={i:w in E_i}. By (1) it is nonempty almost everywhere.
In fact the finite union of the closed E_i contains every sampled fiber:
an omitted relative-open part of a positive fiber would have positive
nu measure. Initial and later zero-measure sets can in any event be
assigned separately without changing any equation in (1).

Choose relative affine coordinates of dimension q for C and write
v(w)=(1,w). For any measurable nonempty allowed-label map I(w), let D(I)
be the vectors of row moments

    b(q)=(integral v(w) q_i(w) dnu(w))_(i=1,...,s)

of allocations with q_i>=0, sum q_i=1, and q_i=0 outside I. This is a
compact convex subset of R^{s(q+1)}. To see compactness, allocations lie
in the bounded weak-star compact set of L-infinity(nu)^s, and positivity,
the sum constraint, and the prescribed zero sets are weak-star closed.
The finitely many bounded moment functions belong to L1(nu), so their
integrals are continuous. Equivalently the elementary L2 compact moment
proof in the earlier full-space allocation theorem applies unchanged.

The desired moment vector is b=(m_i(1,Y_i))_i. The initial feasibility
hypothesis says b belongs to D(I_0). Since all row moments sum to the
fixed total target moment, its affine dimension is at most
(s-1)(q+1); it may be much smaller.

## 3. Exact facial reduction by affine winners

Suppose b is on the RELATIVE boundary of a current moment range D.
Within aff D choose a nonconstant supporting linear functional theta
whose maximum is attained at b. Write its label scores as

    s_i(w)=theta_i.v(w).

The support function of D is exactly

    h_D(theta)=integral max_(i in I(w)) s_i(w) dnu(w).  (4)

Measurably assign each point to its first maximizing label to attain the
right side. An allocation q lies in the exposed face
D intersect {theta.b'=theta.b} if and only if, almost everywhere, it
uses only labels attaining that pointwise maximum. Indeed its support
gap is the integral of

    sum_i q_i(w)[max_(j in I(w))s_j(w)-s_i(w)]>=0;

zero integral is exactly the stated condition. Therefore the exposed
face is ITSELF exactly D(I_new), where

    I_new(w)=argmax_(i in I(w)) s_i(w).                 (5)

This is an equality of moment ranges, not merely containment. All
allocations realizing b already obey (5), so no feasible desired row
moments are lost.

Because the supporting functional was nonconstant on aff D, the new
range has strictly smaller affine dimension. Repeat until b lies in
the relative interior. This takes at most dim D(I_0) reductions, even
if labels have repeated affine spans, disconnected allowed regions, or
some faces have zero measure. A reduction which changes only null sets
would not change D and thus cannot be selected as a proper reduction.
A zero-dimensional D already has b in its relative interior.

Each step uses finitely many affine score comparisons. Combined with
(3), they give a finite affine hyperplane arrangement on every sampled
fiber. On each full d-dimensional chamber all comparisons have fixed
sign or are identically equal, and the final label set I_*(w) is constant.
If two scores agree on an entire fiber, keep BOTH tied labels; do not
discard that fiber as a null hyperplane. Lower-dimensional strata in a
positive fiber have zero d-volume and are immaterial to its moments.
This also explains why lower affine-span degeneracies cause no failure
of finite termination.

## 4. Attained entropy dual on the correct quotient

Put D_*=D(I_*), V=span(D_*-D_*), and note b in relint D_*. Consider

    F(theta)=integral log[sum_(i in I_*(w)) exp(theta_i.v(w))] dnu
                                                    -theta.b. (6)

The genuine gauge space is V-perp, which can be larger than adding the
same affine score to every label. If g lies in V-perp, its functional
is constant on D_*. Applying (4) to g and -g shows

    integral [max_(i in I_*) g_i.v-min_(i in I_*) g_i.v] dnu=0.

Thus all allowed g scores agree pointwise almost everywhere. Their common
integral is g.b. It follows that F(theta+g)=F(theta). This handles every
repeated-span and disconnected-label gauge without an unjustified
full-dimensional moment assumption.

Restrict theta to V. Relative interior gives r>0 with
b+r times the unit ball of V contained in D_*. Hence

    F(theta)>=h_D*(theta)-theta.b>=r ||theta||,
    F(theta)<=h_D*(theta)-theta.b+nu(S) log s.          (7)

These inequalities use max score <= log-sum-exp <= max score+log s.
Consequently F is coercive on V and attains a finite minimizer theta_*.
If V={0}, take theta_*=0. In particular one may choose
||theta_*||<=nu(S) log(s)/r when V is nonzero.

The function F is smooth: v is bounded, nu finite, and differentiation
of log-sum-exp on compact theta sets is dominated by constants. Its
gradient is

    grad F(theta)=b(q_theta)-b,

where q_theta is (2) using theta's scores and I_*. This gradient lies
in V because both moment vectors lie in D_*. At the minimum on V it
also lies in V-perp. Therefore it is zero and q_theta* has EXACTLY the
required masses and full first moments.

One can additionally check strict convexity on V. Its second derivative
in direction xi is the integral of the softmax variance of xi_i.v.
It vanishes only if these scores agree for all allowed labels almost
everywhere, which means xi lies in V-perp. Thus a nonzero xi in V has
strictly positive second derivative. The quotient minimizer is unique;
no uniqueness of the original martingale allocation was assumed.

## 5. Contact, smooth pieces, and entropy optimality

Final allowed labels are subsets of the initial ones, so all original
source contact requirements are retained. In particular each row also
has its prescribed L moment: on any active source plane A_r, row contact
gives L=A_r almost everywhere, and its barycenter gives
integral L q_i dnu=m_i L(Y_i).

Formula (2) is an affine-score softmax on each chamber. Its denominator
is positive everywhere and the scores are bounded on compact C. For a
fixed theorem instance every permitted q_i on a chamber is bounded below
by a positive constant depending on theta_* and C. All derivatives of
every fixed order are bounded on its closure by the same affine-score
formula. In a cell where L=A_r, positivity on compact C gives A_r bounded
away from zero there and on a small neighborhood. Consequently the
density q_i/(M A_r) has an analytic extension and bounded derivatives
on that closure as well. This explicitly handles the PL creases of the
target density; global smoothness across them is not assumed.

The obtained allocation is the unique conditional-entropy maximizer
among feasible allocations, modulo nu-null sets. Indeed all feasible
allocations with moments b obey every facial restriction above. On the
final labels, log q_i*=theta_i*.v-log Z(w); its integral against ANY
feasible q has the same value. Thus

    entropy(q*)-entropy(q)
       =integral sum_i q_i log(q_i/q_i*) dnu>=0.       (8)

Equality forces q=q* almost everywhere. This entropy statement is a
consequence of the construction, not an extra feasibility assumption.

## 6. Sampled boundary traces and unavoidable jumps

There are finitely many chambers. Their analytic extensions give a
one-sided trace on every incident cell closure. Across an internal affine
wall two traces can differ; no common value or cancellation of their
distributional jump is asserted. On the EXTERNAL convex fiber boundary
there is a unique interior trace at surface-almost-every point. A cutting
hyperplane which properly crosses K has surface-null intersection with
its boundary. If it supports K, its positive-area boundary part has only
one interior side. With finitely many hyperplanes, their remaining
intersections and edges are surface-null; for d=1 use the unique interior
interval at each endpoint. Thus the stated trace assertion includes flat
facets and nonsmooth convex fibers.

Boundary versions can be assigned using these traces where unique and
any incident full-dimensional chamber elsewhere, with a finite measurable
tie rule. Original contact sets are closed, so each such trace still uses
only original contacting labels and sums to one. Changes on these null
sets do not change (1). Final facial argmax restrictions are only needed
nu-almost everywhere, and need not be separately reimposed on a chosen
boundary version. One can instead retain their pointwise softmax version;
its values on a null wall need not equal its interior trace.

Global continuity is generally IMPOSSIBLE. Let n=0,d=1,K=[-1,1], L=1,
dnu=dx/2, with two sources Y_-=-1/2,Y_+=1/2 and masses m_-=m_+=1/2.
These have an exact contact martingale

    q_+=1_(x>0),       q_-=1_(x<0).

For any feasible q_+, its mass is 1/2 and its first moment must be 1/4,
the maximum possible among 0<=q<=1 of that mass. In fact

    1/4-integral x q(x) dx/2
      =integral_(0,1) x[1-q(x)] dx/2
         +integral_(-1,0) (-x)q(x) dx/2 >=0.           (9)

Equality forces the displayed indicator almost everywhere. No globally
continuous feasible allocation exists. Facial reduction separates the
two half-intervals, after which their one-label softmaxes are exactly
these indicators. This is an actual uniform convex-body calibration,
not an arbitrary target density.

## 7. Limits of the conclusion

The theorem proves finite piecewise-analytic EXACT allocations, with full
moments and all source contacts. It does not yield globally differentiable
row fields, uniform derivative bounds over varying moment data, or a
row-specific physical push preserving compatibility. Any such push must
retain internal jump fluxes and actual boundary traces; it cannot simply
differentiate the softmax in each chamber and ignore the interfaces.
